source_curriculum.instruction: Treat the actual Python lesson files as the canonical source for sequence, learning objectives, example datasets, expected outputs, exercises, and assessment criteria. This JSON records the intended unit-by-unit correspondence; when a lesson title or subtopic differs from the live Python file, inspect the live source and preserve its actual content.

curriculum_goal: Create functionally equivalent introductory computer science courses in different general-purpose programming languages. Students should encounter the same concepts, problem contexts, datasets, input/output behavior, edge cases, project specifications, and assessment expectations. The primary variable between courses should be the language syntax, type system, runtime, standard library, idioms, and language-specific semantics—not a different set of examples or problem domains.

HTML_CSS.reason: HTML structures semantic documents and CSS controls presentation; these have distinct learning objectives and accessibility requirements.

R.reason: R is taught for statistical computing, data analysis, visualization, and reproducible research; use datasets and statistical questions appropriate to that domain.

SQL.reason: SQL is declarative and relational; teach schemas, relations, queries, joins, constraints, transactions, and query reasoning rather than procedural-language lesson equivalence.

equivalence_rules: Preserve the same unit order and the same learning objective in every general-purpose track.
Preserve the same example problem, input values, dataset, boundary cases, and expected output wherever technically possible.
Use idiomatic language syntax; never produce awkward literal translations solely to resemble Python.
When a language has no direct equivalent, teach the closest idiomatic construct and explicitly explain the semantic difference.
Do not introduce unrelated examples that make the learner solve a new domain problem while learning new syntax.
Keep code examples small, runnable, and independently understandable; introduce complexity incrementally.
For compiled languages, include compile and run commands and explain compiler diagnostics. For interpreted languages, explain interpreter execution.
For statically typed languages, explicitly teach type declarations/inference and conversion. For memory-safe or ownership-oriented languages, explain ownership/borrowing where relevant.
For C and C++, include memory, arrays, pointers/references, and resource-lifetime lessons without changing the shared problem context.
For Julia, emphasize arrays, broadcasting, multiple dispatch, and numerical workloads while retaining shared general-programming examples.
For Rust, explain ownership, borrowing, Result/Option, and traits in the context of the shared examples.
For Swift, explain optionals, value semantics, protocols, and Codable in the context of the shared examples.
For Go, explain packages, slices, maps, structs, interfaces, explicit errors, and concurrency as appropriate.
For Lua, explain tables, dynamic values, functions as values, modules, and metatables using the shared examples.

Every general-purpose track assumes the learner has completed Unit P (FOUNDATIONS/unit-p-computing-foundations.md) and may refer to it by lesson number instead of repeating language-neutral definitions.

accessibility_requirements: Keyboard-first instructions; do not require mouse-only operation.
Ensure code and output can be read sequentially with screen readers and braille displays.
Explain punctuation, indentation, braces, delimiters, and nesting when they affect code interpretation.
Do not use color as the only way to communicate meaning.
Use descriptive prompts and explicit textual errors; provide textual equivalents for charts and visual outputs.
Include terminal execution paths even when an IDE run command exists.
Test examples with common screen-reader workflows where practical; do not claim testing unless it was performed.

course_quality_gates: Every unit 0–11 exists in each general-purpose course.
Every Python lesson has an explicit mapped counterpart or a documented language-specific reason for adaptation.
Every substantive lesson contains a worked example, expected behavior, common mistakes, activities, accessibility practice, and a skills checklist.
The same shared datasets and expected results are used across parallel tracks.
Examples compile or execute under the documented language version; do not claim validation unless actually run.
All code uses idiomatic conventions for the target language and explains non-equivalent constructs.
The course includes text adventure, command-line to-do, and personal-data manager projects with equivalent requirements.
The final assessment checks understanding of the target language rather than visual IDE fluency.
AI policy is consistent: AI may support personal conceptual understanding and reinforcement only; it may not write, autocomplete, repair, complete, or generate course code or assessment solutions.
